tier_reason: docs/benchmark.rst compares nanobind against pybind11, pybind11+smart_holder, Boost.Python, Cython and cppyy; the generating and timing code is public in docs/microbenchmark.ipynb, which gives the full clang++ 15.0.7 command line (-march=native -std=c++17 -fPIC -fno-stack-protector; -O0 -g3 debug, -Os -g0 opt), and the page names the CPU (AMD Ryzen 9 7950X, boost off, clocks pinned, median of 5).

corrections.claimed_speedup: Per-bar labels in the page's SVG plots (ratios relative to nanobind). Compile time: vs pybind11 2.3-3.1x (2.7x func, 3.1x class in -Os builds), vs pybind11+smart_holder 2.3-4.0x, vs Boost.Python 1.4-3.4x, vs Cython 1.6-4.4x except func [debug] where Cython compiles faster (x0.8). The page prose says '~2.7-4.4x vs pybind11', but the 4.4x label belongs to Cython's class [opt] column; the pybind11 maximum is 3.1x (4.0x with smart_holder). Binary size in -Os builds: vs pybind11 3.3-3.7x (smart_holder 3.7-4.9x), vs Boost.Python 9.4-10.9x, vs Cython 3.3-12.5x (in the func debug build Cython is smaller, x0.4). Runtime for a bound call loop in -Os builds: vs pybind11 3.0x (func: 1.80 s vs 0.61 s for 10M calls) and 10.1x (class: 3.06 s vs 0.30 s for 2.5M construct+sum), 13.7x and 22.5x in debug builds; vs Boost.Python 2.2x/4.4x; vs cppyy 1.6x/2.1x; Cython 1.1x slower on func but about 1.4x faster on class (0.21 s vs 0.30 s, derived from page data).
corrections.workload: Generated binding microbenchmark: function-heavy module of 720 trivial functions (all permutations of six integer/float argument types) and class-heavy module of 252 small structs with constructor and sum() (the generator stops after i > 250, so not 720); compile time and stripped binary size of each module, and runtime of calling test_0000 10M times and constructing Struct0 + sum() 2.5M times, each in debug (-O0 -g3) and size-optimised (-Os -g0) builds, median of 5 runs.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: clang++ 15.0.7 -march=native -shared -std=c++17 -fPIC -fno-stack-protector -Wno-deprecated-declarations -DPYBIND11_USE_SMART_HOLDER_AS_DEFAULT, plus -O0 -g3 (debug) or -Os -g0 (opt, then stripped); same command for every library (docs/microbenchmark.ipynb). Python 3.10.6, cppyy 1.12.13, Cython 0.29.28, nanobind 1.2.0; pybind11 and Boost.Python versions not stated (pybind11 built from a local git checkout).
corrections.caveats: Numbers come from nanobind 1.2.0, Python 3.10 and one workstation, measured by the author; they measure binding overhead on trivial functions, not application speed. The 'opt' builds use -Os, not -O2/-O3, and -march=native. The page's prose '2.7-4.4x vs pybind11' compile-time range is slightly overstated versus its own plot labels (pybind11 max 3.1x, smart_holder 4.0x). The '~10x lower runtime overhead' holds for the class benchmark only (about 3x for plain function calls), and Cython is about 1.4x faster than nanobind in the class runtime test. pybind11 and Boost versions are unpinned. Harness quirks that do not affect the pybind11 comparison: the Boost.Python class bindings declare init with the fifth argument type twice, and the pure-Python reference Struct0.sum omits field d. The baseline is not one of the category's listed incumbents (Lua, Duktape, QuickJS), and nanobind extends CPython from C++ rather than embedding a script engine, so a category move (FFI/bindings) is plausible.

notes: Tier A holds: public notebook with exact compiler command and named CPU. Correct the compile-time range to the plot labels (2.3-3.1x vs pybind11 overall, 2.7-3.1x in -Os builds) and record that the 10x runtime figure is class-only and that Cython wins the class runtime test; metadata (BSD-3-Clause, 3.7k stars, last commit 2026-09-28, not a fork) confirmed. Consider moving it out of embedded-scripting into an FFI/bindings category.

tier_reason: Upgraded D to C: the author's benchmark page (readthedocs/ravi-benchmarks.rst, still on the archived llvm branch) and the 2015 Lua Workshop slides in the repo give timings against Lua 5.3 and LuaJIT 2.1, with benchmark programs public in tests/performance; first-party, and no CPU model or compiler flags (only Windows 10 64-bit, LLVM 3.9, Visual C++ 2015), so not A or B.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Ravi with the (now archived) LLVM JIT vs Lua 5.3.2, JIT compile time excluded: fornum_test1 8.94 s vs 0.309 s (about 29x), fornum_test3 52.494 s vs 4.748 s (about 11x), fornum_test2 about 2.1x; untyped Lua code gains only 1.6-2.5x (mandel1.lua 20.324 vs 8.056 s, fannkuchen.lua 46.203 vs 28.422 s, matmul1.lua 26.672 vs 16.83 s); with Ravi type annotations about 13x on mandel (1.571 s), 10x on fannkuchen (4.634 s) and 26x on matmul (1.039 s, array read bounds checks disabled) relative to the untyped Lua 5.3.2 run (ratios derived from page data). Typed Ravi roughly matches LuaJIT 2.1 (1.594, 4.672, 1.078 s) but is far slower than LuaJIT on untyped code. The Ravi interpreter alone is within about 5% of Lua 5.3.2. The 2015 Lua Workshop slides show similar numbers (e.g. matmul(1000) 34.604 s Lua 5.3 vs 1.018 s Ravi LLVM).
corrections.workload: Numeric micro-benchmarks in tests/performance (fornum loop tests, mandel1 at 4000, fannkuchen at 11, matmul1 at 1000), each as plain Lua and as Ravi-typed variants, timed under Lua 5.3.2, the Ravi interpreter, Ravi with the LLVM JIT, and LuaJIT 2.1 interpreter and JIT.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Ravi and Lua 5.3.2 compiled with Visual C++ 2015 (flags not stated); LLVM 3.9 JIT backend.
corrections.caveats: All numbers are the author's own, from about 2016 (Lua 5.3.2, LLVM 3.9, Visual C++ 2015, Windows 10) with no CPU or flags given. They measure the LLVM JIT backend, which the README says is archived; the current MIR backend has no published numbers that were found, so today's performance is unverified. JIT compilation time is excluded, the large wins need Ravi type annotations (untyped Lua code gains only 1.6-2.5x), and matmul ran with array read bounds checks disabled. The README says Ravi favours maintainability, safety and Lua 5.3 compatibility over maximum performance, and LuaJIT 2.1 is as fast or faster on every benchmark. The benchmark page is no longer in master's readthedocs folder (only on the llvm branch; the readthedocs.io copy is blocked here, its numbers were confirmed from a search snippet and the branch file).

notes: Upgrade D to C: numbers exist in readthedocs/ravi-benchmarks.rst on the llvm branch and in readthedocs/ravi-luaconf-2015.pdf on master, against Lua 5.3.2 (in-list baseline) with benchmark code in tests/performance. Main shortcomings: measured on the archived LLVM backend with JIT time excluded and typed code only, no CPU/flags, no numbers for the current MIR JIT. Metadata (MIT, 1.3k stars, last commit 2026-09-12, not a fork) confirmed.
